messages:
elaine: starting a quick thread to land a per-org rate policy we can ship this quarter. idea is: RPM/TPM + concurrency cap + a small burst-credit system. want enforcement and observable UX. thoughts?

max: +1. we need both steady-rate (rpm/tpm) and a burst bucket. burst should be sized by org tier. simple token-bucket refill per second works.

nina: high level Q: what are our latency/availability goals when someone hits the cap? do we 1) reject immediately, 2) queue at router, or 3) fallback to cheaper model? different behaviors have different UX/telemetry implications.

tom: prefer fast fail at the edge for non-critical paths. router-level reject (HTTP 429) keeps resources predictable. we can support router->aggregator backpressure for dedicated customers that want queueing.

elaine: agree. public hosted: immediate 429. dedicated/private: optional queueing + canary fallback to smaller model. Also need to decide precedence when both RPM and concurrency are near limits.

max: proposal (rough):
```yaml
policy:
  org_id: <org>
  rpm: 60000      # requests per minute
  tpm: 1_200_000  # tokens per minute (for tokenized billing)
  concurrency: 200
  burst_credits: 500   # tokens that can be spent quickly
  burst_window_sec: 60 # window to refill credits
  enforcement_point: router # router | aggregator
```
This keeps rules explicit and makes console surface straightforward.

nina: telemetry requirements: per-org meters for: rpm_used, tpm_used, concurrency_current, burst_credits_remaining, last_reject_reason. also sample traces at 5-10% for 429s and fallbacks. Need metric names and tags (org_id, route, model).

tom: enforcement detail: router must make an O(1) check. keep policy cache in env, avoid db lookup on hot path. For concurrency we need a distributed counter (redis/etcd). TTLs are tricky when workers die. Suggest using lease-based counters + occasional reconciliation.

elaine: good call. also UX: console should show a small timeline and projected depletion time for burst credits. admins can top-up or request emergency burst (manual or via policy). show current enforcement point and last 24h rejects.

max: billing interaction: if burst credits allow temporary overspend, we should surface "burst usage" as a separate line item in billing dashboard and optionally bill overage or throttle. defaults: sandbox orgs get higher relative burst.

nina: security/segmentation: for Private deployments, default rpm/concurrency should be higher and enforcement point may be inside customer VPC. Default policy template must be configurable per-deployment.

ratebot: NOTICE: policy draft posted to #infra-policies repo in branch per-org-burst. PR: https://git.internal/redwood/infra-policies/pull/412 (staging-only).

elaine: open questions:
- exact token math: do we count tokens (for tpm) separately from requests (for rpm)? think yes — both enforced.
- burst credit unit: token vs request? prefer token to align with billing.
- concurrency vs rpm precedence: proposal: concurrency check first (reject if at cap), rpm/tpm second (token-bucket).

max: i support concurrency-first. otherwise a flash of long-running requests could eat burst credits and tank p95. concurrency-first protects latency.

nina: telemetry action: i'll add metric names and dashboards. will also add an alert when burst depletion rate > 50 credits/min for > 5m.

tom: action: i'll prototype router enforcement using local in-memory token-bucket + redis counter for concurrency. will add reconciliation job.

elaine: action: i'll draft the console UX mockups and an ops playbook for emergency top-ups/fallbacks.

max: timeline: PR for enforcement by end of sprint (2w). telemetry + dashboard next sprint.

nina: ack :thumbsup:

aelaine: thanks all. ping me if you need spec details.

ratebot: DEPLOY: staging policy sync applied for org=internal-test at 1887654385.
